title: The k Strongest Values in an Array
statement:
You get an integer array `arr` and an integer `k`. Let `m` be the median of `arr`, defined as the value at index `(n - 1) / 2` (rounded down, 0-indexed) once `arr` is sorted in ascending order, where `n` is its length.

Compare two values by their distance from the median: `x` beats `y` when `|x - m| > |y - m|`, and when the two distances are equal, the larger of `x` and `y` wins. Return the `k` values of `arr` that rank highest under this order (repeated values count separately). The returned list may be in any order.
notes:
## Intuition

The direct route is to find the median, sort every value by "distance from the median, then by value", and keep the first `k`. But once `arr` itself is sorted, the strongest remaining value is always at one of the two ends: values get closer to the median as you walk inward from either side. So two pointers can peel off the winners one at a time without a custom comparator.

## Approach

1. Sort `arr` ascending and read `median` at index `(n - 1) / 2`, rounded down.
2. Put `left` on the first index and `right` on the last.
3. While `result` holds fewer than `k` values, compute `leftGap` and `rightGap`, the distances of the two end values from `median`.
4. If `rightGap >= leftGap`, the right value wins (on a tie it is the larger value), so push it and move `right` inward; otherwise push the left value and move `left` inward.
5. Return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, `k = 2`. It is already sorted and `median = arr[2] = 3`.

- `left = 0` (value 1, gap 2), `right = 4` (value 5, gap 2). Tie, so take `5`; `right = 3`.
- Value 1 has gap 2, value 4 has gap 1. The left side wins: take `1`; `left = 1`.

`result = [5, 1]` has `k` values, so it is returned.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the two-pointer phase takes only `k` steps.
- Space: O(k) for `result`, plus whatever the sort uses.

## Pitfalls

- The median is the element at index `(n - 1) / 2` of the sorted array, not the average of the two middle values for even `n`.
- On equal gaps the larger value wins; with `arr` sorted that is always the right end, so the comparison must be `>=`, not `>`.
- Compute the median after sorting; reading the middle of the unsorted input gives a wrong centre.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `median` | the centre value every distance is measured from |
| `left`, `right` | ends of the not-yet-taken part of the sorted array |
| `leftGap`, `rightGap` | distances of `arr[left]` and `arr[right]` from `median` |
| `result` | the strongest values taken so far |

narration.2: Sort the values so the strongest remaining one is always at an end.
narration.3: The median is the sorted element at index (n - 1) / 2, rounded down.
narration.5: left marks the smallest value not taken yet.
narration.6: right marks the largest value not taken yet.
narration.8: Keep taking values until k of them are collected.
narration.9: How far the smallest remaining value is from the median.
narration.10: How far the largest remaining value is from the median.
narration.11: The right value wins when it is at least as far away, because on a tie the larger value is stronger.
narration.15: Otherwise the left value is strictly farther, so take it...
narration.19: result now holds the k strongest values.
